identification.summary: Velvet Tempest is Microsoft's name for a financially motivated ransomware affiliate group that Microsoft previously tracked as DEV-0504; Microsoft's June 2022 BlackCat reporting describes it as an active affiliate that had switched to the BlackCat (ALPHV) RaaS payload [S1]. Microsoft's April 2023 update to that article states DEV-0504 is now tracked as Velvet Tempest [S1]. Secondary coverage of a March 2026 MalBeacon report says the group has been involved in ransomware as an affiliate for at least five years and is linked to Ryuk, REvil, Conti, BlackMatter, BlackCat/ALPHV, LockBit and RansomHub payloads [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft (June 2022) used BlackCat from December 2021 for this affiliate and noted earlier use of Ryuk, REvil, BlackMatter, Conti and LockBit 2.0 [S1]. A search-result summary of Microsoft's reporting says DEV-0504 has been active since 2020 [S4]; not confirmed in the page text read.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Velvet Tempest (formerly DEV-0504) [S1]. The encyclopedia record also lists CrowdStrike ALPHA SPIDER; however, search results describe ALPHA SPIDER as the actor behind the ALPHV/BlackCat RaaS itself, which is a different thing from a BlackCat affiliate, so that alias mapping should be verified and not treated as an equivalence of facts. Headlines of March 2026 tying the activity to 'Termite ransomware' overstate the evidence: no encryption was observed and the Termite link is based on infrastructure overlap [S2][S3].

attribution.sponsor: Financially motivated criminal affiliate; no state sponsor identified in the sources gathered [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's own naming and its observation of DEV-0504 as a BlackCat affiliate are stated in [S1]. MalBeacon (as reported by secondary outlets) characterized the March 2026 activity as consistent with Velvet Tempest and its Termite ecosystem, not as confirmed ransomware deployment [S2][S3]. Confidence level is not stated numerically in the sources read.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry-based tracking of the DEV-0504 affiliate cluster [S1]; MalBeacon deception-environment observation and infrastructure overlap (a PowerShell script hosted on an IP linked to Termite tool staging), as relayed by press [S2][S3].

objectives: Financial gain through ransomware extortion, deploying whichever RaaS payload is available; Microsoft notes a pattern of shifting payloads when a RaaS program shuts down [S1][S4]. Data exfiltration with StealBit supports double extortion [S1].

sectors: Fashion, tobacco, IT and manufacturing (per a summary of Microsoft's BlackCat reporting) [S4]
Non-profit (emulated U.S. non-profit environment in the 2026 MalBeacon observation; a honeypot, not a real victim) [S2]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's page text read did not itself list sectors or geographies for DEV-0504 [S1]; sector list comes from a secondary summary [S4]. No region data gathered.

capabilities.summary: Per Microsoft (2022): initial access via remote sign-in with compromised credentials, domain reconnaissance, lateral movement with the compromised account, credential theft with Mimikatz and Rubeus, data exfiltration with StealBit (often renamed send.exe or sender.exe), and ransomware distribution with PsExec [S1]. 2026 MalBeacon observation (via press): malvertising leading to a ClickFix fake-CAPTCHA lure that has the victim paste an obfuscated command into the Windows Run dialog, Active Directory and host reconnaissance, PowerShell harvesting of Chrome-stored credentials, and staging of DonutLoader and CastleRAT [S2][S3]. Affiliate model: moves between RaaS programs (Ryuk, REvil, Conti, BlackMatter, LockBit 2.0, BlackCat) [S1].

campaigns.name: Adoption of BlackCat (ALPHV) payload
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports DEV-0504 as an affiliate that had switched to BlackCat, with use dating from December 2021, after prior use of BlackMatter, Conti, LockBit 2.0, REvil and Ryuk.

campaigns.name: Microsoft publication on BlackCat affiliates
campaigns.summary: Microsoft describes DEV-0504 intrusion chain: compromised-credential remote access, Mimikatz and Rubeus, StealBit exfiltration, PsExec deployment.

campaigns.name: Rename to Velvet Tempest
campaigns.summary: Microsoft updates its article to state DEV-0504 is now tracked as Velvet Tempest.

campaigns.name: MalBeacon ClickFix, DonutLoader and CastleRAT intrusion
campaigns.summary: In a 12-day observation in an emulated U.S. non-profit environment (reported as starting 3 February), malvertising and ClickFix led to AD reconnaissance, Chrome credential theft, DonutLoader staging and CastleRAT. No encryption was observed; the Termite link rests on infrastructure overlap.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated ransomware affiliate tracked by Microsoft as Velvet Tempest (ex-DEV-0504) [S1].
diamond.capability: Mimikatz, Rubeus, StealBit, PsExec, ClickFix lures, DonutLoader, CastleRAT; rotating RaaS payloads [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Malvertising delivery and a hosted PowerShell script on an IP linked to Termite staging, per press reporting of MalBeacon [S2][S3]. Specific IOCs not gathered.
diamond.victim: Organizations in fashion, tobacco, IT and manufacturing (secondary summary) [S4]; honeypot non-profit in 2026 [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Criminal RaaS ecosystem; affiliates move between programs as programs are disrupted or shut down [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows domain environments, remote-access services accepting compromised credentials, and user-executed Run-dialog commands [S1][S2].

gaps: Primary MalBeacon report was not opened; WebFetch could not reach bleepingcomputer.com, vpncentral.com, scworld.com or Malpedia from this environment, so 2026 details rely on search-result summaries.
Microsoft's Velvet Tempest-specific actor page was not found; naming history relies on the 2022 article with its April 2023 update [S1].
Victimology, geography and ransom amounts are not established in the sources gathered.
Whether Velvet Tempest used RansomHub (S-RM coverage mentions it, undated in the result) and Termite is unverified; the Termite relationship is infrastructure-based only.
CrowdStrike ALPHA SPIDER appears to denote the ALPHV/BlackCat operators, not an affiliate; the encyclopedia alias needs validation against CrowdStrike.
Sector list [S4] comes from a secondary summary of Microsoft's reporting; the Microsoft page text read did not list sectors.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is domain-joined Windows networks, remote-access services and user workstations with browsers storing credentials [S1][S2]. STEP 2: Affiliate behavior changes with the RaaS market, so payload-based signatures age quickly; the intrusion chain is more stable [S1]. STEP 3: Template is compromised credentials or ClickFix lure, AD reconnaissance, credential theft, StealBit exfiltration, PsExec ransomware deployment [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued ransomware affiliate intrusions against commercial and non-profit organizations, including DIB suppliers. MDCOA is disruptive encryption of a defense contractor or base-support network. Candidate indicators: Run-dialog paste commands from browsers, PowerShell reading Chrome credential stores, StealBit-like binaries named send.exe or sender.exe, PsExec bursts across hosts [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track affiliate payload shifts and ClickFix-style lures as leading indicators for user-awareness and EDR tuning. (2) Authorities: criminal activity against non-DoD networks falls to law-enforcement and DC3/DIB partnership channels, not DoD offensive action. (3) Mission assurance: protect remote-access credentials and back up critical mission systems against double-extortion. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DIB partners and CISA-type reporting channels.
